meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'сделать'.

examples.trans: Hi, Arkady Borisovich. What are you doing?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'well; come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Это хорошо, что готово. А то мы уже начали беспокоиться.
examples.trans: It's good that it's ready. We were starting to worry.

examples.text: А если я не скажу, то что? Ты мне ухо отрежешь?
examples.trans: And if I don't tell you, then what? Will you cut my ear off?

examples.text: А если я не скажу, то что?
examples.trans: And if I don't tell you, then what?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'oneself', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А с Пашей я снова чувствую себя женщиной.
examples.trans: And with Pasha I feel like a woman again.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'нести'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'will bring', paired with 'приносить'.

examples.text: А я вот вам чаю с сушками принёс.
examples.trans: I've brought you some tea and bread rings.

examples.text: А что это ты в квартиру принёс?
examples.trans: And what is that you brought into the flat?

examples.text: Видишь, Аркаша, он собаку принёс тебе.
examples.trans: See, Arkasha, he brought you a dog.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Подождите! Два дня — это же очень мало.
examples.trans: Hold on! Two days is far too little.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'whether, if; (что ли) or what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I don't know whether he is at home.
Was it Osipenko who hired you?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'house; building; home' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: There's a new building on Simashko Street.

examples.text: Квартира будет отличная. На Симашко есть новый дом.
examples.trans: It'll be an excellent flat. There's a new building on Simashko Street.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'can, to be able', paired with 'смочь'.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лучиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to happen', paired with 'случаться'.

examples.text: Марина, я вам обещаю: со стеной ничего не случится.
examples.trans: Marina, I promise you: nothing will happen to the wall.

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'ойти'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to come up (to), to approach', paired with 'подходить'.

examples.text: Нам не нужна ваша приставка! Ещё раз подойдёте к моему ребёнку — пожалеете!
examples.trans: We don't need your console! Come near my child again and you'll be sorry!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The white one? Give me the keys.

examples.text: Мы сюда зачем прилетели? Я сразу сказал: с ним ничего не получится.
examples.trans: What did we even fly out here for? I said from the start: nothing will come of it with him.
Why did you even come here? Empty-handed!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'so, then; like that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'go, walk', paired with 'пойти'.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

examples.text: Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: That's why I'm running for a second term.

examples.text: А ты иди на биржу труда. Там есть работа.
examples.trans: You go to the job centre. There's work there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'over, above; at', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The lamp is above the table.

examples.text: За поведение? Вы смеётесь надо мной?
examples.trans: For my conduct? Are you laughing at me?

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'смотр'). Common masculine noun meaning 'supervision, oversight' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Ты оставил незнакомца совсем одного без присмотра?
examples.trans: You left a stranger completely alone without supervision?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for; behind', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'no; there isn't', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'until, before; up to', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

related.gloss: to reach, walk as far as

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'evening' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Добрый вечер, Вика. С Новым годом!
examples.trans: Good evening, Vika. Happy New Year!

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to find', paired with 'находить'.

examples.text: Ну где я сейчас найду грузчиков?
examples.trans: Well, where am I going to find movers right now?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian cardinal or ordinal numeral meaning 'a hundred', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I've got a hundred and ten.

examples.text: Понимаешь, Аркаша, мы все скидываемся на этот кластер. Мне москвичам сегодня надо отдать сто пятьдесят.
examples.trans: You see, Arkasha, we're all chipping in for this cluster. I have to give the Moscow people a hundred and fifty today.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'thousand' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Мы построим кластер. Это тысячи рабочих мест.
examples.trans: We will build the cluster. That means thousands of jobs.

meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'ллар'). Common masculine noun meaning 'dollar' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The ticket costs a hundred dollars.

examples.text: Возьмите! Они десять тысяч долларов стоят!
examples.trans: Take it! It costs ten thousand dollars!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to run, to flee', paired with 'побежать'.

examples.trans: Run, Marina, before it's too late!
Where are you running so fast?

examples.text: Надо бежать! Беги в деревню к маме.
examples.trans: You need to run! Run to the village to your mum's.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to know'.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'anywhere, somewhere', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Куда-нибудь, шеф меня только что уволил.
examples.trans: Anywhere, the chef just fired me.

examples.text: Слушай, а может мы сходим куда-нибудь?
examples.trans: Listen, maybe we should go somewhere?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
Common masculine noun meaning 'address' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I'll give the address: seven Sadovaya Street.

meanings.en: to speak, to say, to talk
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to speak, to say, to talk', paired with 'сказать'.
Common Russian noun meaning 'kids; guys' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Тогда ребята с тобой поработают. До свидания, Аркадий Борисович.
examples.trans: Then the boys will have a little word with you. Goodbye, Arkady Borisovich.
Then the boys will have a little word with you.
Right, kids, go out of the room.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'where to', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Wait, where are you two going?

examples.text: Хорошо. Значит, вот куда идут деньги налогоплательщиков.
examples.trans: Fine. So this is where taxpayers' money goes.

examples.text: Значит, вот куда идут деньги налогоплательщиков.
examples.trans: So this is where taxpayers' money goes.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning '(emphasis) after all, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'child' in everyday Russian.
Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лушать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to listen', paired with 'послушать'.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, I've been thinking. Your boss is such an experienced specialist.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes, indeed', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

Prefix 'рас-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'слабиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to relax', paired with 'расслабляться'.

examples.text: Ваня, расслабься. В этот раз без обмана.
examples.trans: Vanya, relax. This time there's no trick.
